chapter.name: Perimeter and Area
chapter.blurb: Revises the perimeter of rectangles, squares and triangles and extends it to regular polygons and to shapes made by cutting and rejoining pieces; introduces the area of rectangles, squares and composite figures, estimating area on a squared grid, the area of a triangle as half of an enclosing rectangle, and the relationship between area and perimeter for a fixed amount of material.

scope_in.item: Perimeter of rectangles, squares and triangles; perimeter of any polygon as the sum of its side lengths
Perimeter of regular polygons (n x side length, including the equilateral triangle) and the effect on perimeter of cutting a shape into pieces and rejoining them differently
Area of rectangles and squares, and finding the area of composite/irregular straight-edged shapes by splitting them into rectangles
Estimating the area of an irregular shape by tracing it onto squared/graph paper and applying the counting convention (full, more than half, exactly half, less than half covered squares)
Area of a triangle as half the area of an enclosing rectangle that shares the same base and height

The relationship between area and perimeter: the same area can give different perimeters and vice versa; minimum/maximum perimeter for a fixed number of unit squares; solving for a missing dimension or area in a composite rectangular figure

concepts.name: Perimeter of rectangles, squares and triangles
concepts.description: The perimeter of a closed figure is the total distance around its boundary; for rectangles, squares and triangles this reduces to simple sum-of-sides formulas.
concepts.idea: Perimeter is always just the sum of the lengths of all the sides of a closed figure, however the figure is described.
concepts.rule: Perimeter of a polygon = sum of the lengths of all its sides. Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + breadth). Perimeter of a square = 4 x side. Perimeter of a triangle = sum of its three sides.
concepts.example: A rectangular tablecloth 3 m long and 2 m wide needs 2 x (3 + 2) = 10 m of lace to go all around it.

Meena's equilateral triangle (12, 12, 12), Raj's (10, 12, 14) and Sara's (6, 15, 15) are all valid triangles, since in each the sum of any two sides exceeds the third. questions.q: A shopkeeper claims that doubling the length of a rectangle while keeping the breadth the same will double its perimeter. Is this claim correct? Justify with an example.
questions.a: Not correct in general. For a rectangle of length l and breadth b, perimeter = 2(l+b). Doubling only l gives 2(2l+b), which is not 2 x 2(l+b) unless b = 0. Example: l = 10, b = 5 gives perimeter 30; doubling l to 20 gives perimeter 2(20+5) = 50, not 60.
s: States the claim is false and explains why using the formula
Gives a numerical example showing the perimeter does not double

s: States length + breadth = 30 from the perimeter

concepts.name: Perimeter of regular polygons and rearranged shapes
concepts.description: A regular polygon has all sides and angles equal, so its perimeter is simply the number of sides times one side's length; cutting and rejoining the pieces of a shape keeps its total area the same but can change its perimeter.
concepts.idea: Because a regular polygon's sides are all equal, its perimeter formula is just (number of sides) x (one side's length); and because perimeter depends on how the boundary is arranged, cutting a shape into pieces and rejoining them differently can give a different perimeter even though no material has been added or removed.
concepts.rule: Perimeter of a regular polygon with n equal sides = n x (length of one side). Perimeter of an equilateral triangle = 3 x side. When the pieces of a shape are cut and rejoined differently, the total area of material stays the same but the perimeter can increase, decrease, or stay the same.
concepts.example: An equilateral triangle with side 7 cm has perimeter 3 x 7 = 21 cm.

concepts.name: Area of rectangles, squares and composite figures
concepts.description: The area of a rectangle or square can be found directly from its length and side; the area of a more complex straight-edged shape is found by splitting it into rectangles.
concepts.idea: Any closed figure made up entirely of straight, right-angled edges can be broken down into a set of rectangles whose areas are easy to compute and then combined by addition or subtraction to get the whole figure's area.
concepts.rule: Area of a rectangle = length x width. Area of a square = side x side. The area of a composite shape = the sum (or difference) of the areas of the rectangles it can be split into.
concepts.example: A 5 m by 4 m floor (20 sq m) with a 3 m square carpet (9 sq m) on it has 20 - 9 = 11 sq m left uncarpeted.

concepts.name: Estimating area on a squared grid
concepts.description: The area of an irregular shape can be estimated by tracing it onto squared or graph paper and counting squares according to a fixed convention for full, more-than-half, exactly-half and less-than-half covered squares.
concepts.idea: Since a curved or irregular boundary cannot be measured exactly using square units, a simple, consistent counting rule turns a messy shape into a countable estimate of its area, and this estimate gets closer to the true area as the grid gets finer.
concepts.rule: On a squared grid: a fully covered square counts as 1 sq unit; a square more than half covered counts as 1 sq unit; a square exactly half covered counts as 1/2 sq unit; a square less than half covered is ignored (counted as 0). The estimated area is the sum of all these counts.
concepts.example: A shape covering 4 full squares and 2 exactly-half squares has estimated area 4 + 2 x (1/2) = 5 sq units.

questions.q: A pond traced on a 1 cm grid covers 12 full squares, 5 squares more than half covered, 3 squares exactly half covered, and 6 squares less than half covered. Estimate the pond's area in sq cm, and state which category of squares does not add anything to the estimate.
questions.a: Area = 12 (full) + 5 (more than half, counted as 1 each) + 3 x 0.5 (half squares) + 0 (less than half, ignored) = 12 + 5 + 1.5 + 0 = 18.5 sq cm. The less-than-half squares add nothing to the estimate.

questions.q: A student traces a leaf shape twice, once on a fine 0.5 cm grid and once on a coarse 2 cm grid. Explain, using the counting rules, why the estimate from the fine grid is usually more accurate, and describe what happens to the 'less than half' and 'more than half' misestimate as the grid gets finer.
questions.a: On a coarser grid, each square is large, so a curved boundary can leave big uncounted or over-counted slivers inside squares that are labelled 'less than half' or 'more than half', causing a bigger error. On a finer grid, the squares are much smaller, so the boundary cuts through each square by only a tiny amount, making the 'less than half' and 'more than half' misestimates much smaller in total, so the overall estimate is closer to the true area.
s: Explains coarse squares create larger errors from partial coverage
Explains finer squares reduce the size of the miscounted boundary regions
Concludes the finer grid gives a more accurate estimate

questions.a: Estimated area = F + M + 0.5 x H = 42. So 30 + M + 0.5 x 8 = 42, giving 30 + M + 4 = 42, so M = 8.
s: Sets up the equation F + M + 0.5H = 42
Substitutes F = 30 and H = 8 to get 34 + M = 42
Solves M = 8

questions.q: A rectangle of exact dimensions 6 cm by 4 cm is traced on a 1 cm grid. Explain why the grid-counting method should give exactly 24 sq cm for this shape, with no partial squares involved at all.
questions.a: Since the rectangle's sides are 6 cm and 4 cm, both whole numbers of grid units, and its edges are straight and aligned with the grid lines, every square inside it is either fully inside or fully outside the rectangle -- there are no partially covered squares, so the full-square count of 6 x 4 = 24 gives the exact area, not just an estimate.
s: States the rectangle's straight, grid-aligned edges leave no partial squares
Concludes the full-square count of 24 gives the exact area

questions.q: Two identical leaf shapes are each traced on a different grid: Grid X has smaller squares than Grid Y. On Grid X, the estimate comes out to 18.5 sq units of Grid X's own square size; on Grid Y, the estimate comes out to 19 sq units of Grid Y's own larger square size. Explain how both estimates can be considered reasonable for the same leaf even though the numbers differ, and which estimate you would trust more, and why.
questions.a: Because the two grids use different-sized squares as their unit, the numeric totals (18.5 vs 19) are not directly comparable as raw numbers -- what matters is how close each estimate is, in real area (say sq cm), to the leaf's true area, once each unit square's real size is accounted for. The finer grid (Grid X) breaks the boundary into smaller pieces, so its 'more/less than half' misestimates are individually smaller, making its estimate, once converted to the same real units, generally the more trustworthy of the two.
s: States the two totals are not directly comparable since the unit square sizes differ
Explains that comparison must be made in real area units, not raw square counts
States the finer grid (Grid X) generally gives a more trustworthy estimate
Justifies this with the reduced size of boundary misestimates on a finer grid

questions.q: A student estimates a shape's area by counting only the full squares and ignoring every partially covered square, treating them all as 0, even the more-than-half ones. Evaluate whether this method will overestimate, underestimate, or correctly estimate the true area, and why.
questions.a: This method will underestimate the true area, because it throws away the more-than-half and exactly-half squares completely, even though those squares are mostly or partly inside the shape and should contribute at least some area to the total.

questions.q: Design a shape on a 1 cm grid, by describing how many full, more-than-half, exactly-half, and less-than-half squares it covers, so that its estimated area comes out to exactly 15 sq cm, using at least one square from each of the four categories.
questions.a: One valid design: 10 full squares, 3 squares more than half covered, 4 squares exactly half covered, and 2 squares less than half covered (which contribute nothing). Estimated area = 10 (full) + 3 (more than half) + 4 x 0.5 (half squares, = 2) + 0 (less than half) = 10 + 3 + 2 + 0 = 15 sq cm.

Chooses a number of exactly-half squares whose half-count completes the total

concepts.name: Area of a triangle as half a rectangle
concepts.description: A triangle that shares a base and a height with a rectangle always has exactly half of that rectangle's area, whether the triangle comes from cutting the rectangle along a diagonal or is formed using an altitude.
concepts.idea: Splitting a rectangle along its diagonal, or splitting a triangle using the perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side, always shows the triangle's area to be half of the area of a rectangle built on the same base and height.
concepts.rule: Area of a triangle formed by a rectangle's diagonal = half of the rectangle's area. More generally, area of a triangle = 1/2 x base x height, where base and height are the base and the perpendicular height of a rectangle enclosing the triangle.
concepts.example: A rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm cut along its diagonal gives two triangles, each of area 1/2 x 10 x 6 = 30 sq cm.

questions.q: A triangle and a rectangle have the same base and the same height. Explain how their areas are related, and use this to find the triangle's area if the rectangle's area is 84 sq cm.
questions.a: A triangle with the same base and height as a rectangle always has half the rectangle's area, because it can be seen as one of the two triangles formed by the rectangle's diagonal. So the triangle's area = 84 divided by 2 = 42 sq cm.

questions.q: A quadrilateral field is split by one of its diagonals into two triangles: one with base 26 m and height 14 m, and the other with the same 26 m base (the diagonal) and height 9 m. Find the total area of the quadrilateral, and explain why using the diagonal as a shared base is a useful strategy for finding the area of an irregular quadrilateral.
questions.a: Area of the first triangle = 1/2 x 26 x 14 = 182 sq m. Area of the second triangle = 1/2 x 26 x 9 = 117 sq m. Total area of the quadrilateral = 182 + 117 = 299 sq m. Using the diagonal as a shared base is useful because it splits any quadrilateral into two triangles, and each triangle's area can be found directly once its height, the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the diagonal, is known -- this turns a shape without a simple area formula into two shapes that do have one.
s: Finds the first triangle's area = 182 sq m
Finds the second triangle's area = 117 sq m

questions.q: A student says, 'Since a triangle is half of a rectangle, a triangle's perimeter must also be half of the corresponding rectangle's perimeter.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is false. The half relationship applies only to area, not perimeter -- a triangle formed from a rectangle's diagonal has one extra side, the diagonal, which is usually longer than either the length or breadth, so its perimeter is not simply half the rectangle's perimeter; for example, a 3-4-5 right triangle from a 3 cm by 4 cm rectangle has perimeter 12 cm, while half the rectangle's perimeter (14 cm) is 7 cm -- they don't match.
s: States the claim is false

Solves for a base value

concepts.name: Relationship between area and perimeter
concepts.description: The same area can be arranged to give many different perimeters, and the same perimeter can enclose many different areas; this idea is used to find the smallest or largest possible perimeter for a fixed number of unit squares and to solve for missing dimensions in composite rectangular figures.
concepts.idea: Area and perimeter are independent of each other: fixing one does not fix the other, so exploring different arrangements of the same building blocks (unit squares, or the rooms of a floor plan) can change the perimeter while the total area stays the same.
concepts.rule: Two closed figures can have the same area with different perimeters, or the same perimeter with different areas. Among arrangements of a fixed number of unit squares joined edge to edge with no holes, a compact, square-like arrangement gives close to the smallest possible perimeter, while a single straight row gives the largest. In a composite rectangular figure, a missing dimension or area can be found from area = length x width together with the other known parts.
concepts.example: Nine unit squares arranged as a 3x3 block have perimeter 12 units, but the same nine squares arranged in a single row have perimeter 20 units.

questions.q: Two closed figures can have the same area but ____ perimeters.
questions.a: different

questions.a: Two shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas
o: Two shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas
Two shapes with the same area must always have the same perimeter
Two shapes with the same perimeter must always have the same area
Area and perimeter always increase or decrease together

With 40 m of fencing (so length + breadth = 20), a square (10 m by 10 m) gives area 100 sq m, while a long narrow rectangle such as 18 m by 2 m gives area only 36 sq m, much less. For a fixed perimeter, a shape closer to a square encloses more area, not a long narrow one.

questions.q: Design a rectangular house plan with a total area of 400 sq ft made of two rooms placed side by side, sharing one full wall: a square bedroom and a rectangular hall. Choose the bedroom's side and the hall's dimensions so the plan works out to exactly 400 sq ft, and find the total perimeter of the combined outer boundary if both rooms are 10 ft tall (i.e. the shared wall is 10 ft).
questions.a: Choose the bedroom as a 10 ft square: area = 100 sq ft. The hall must then have area 400 - 100 = 300 sq ft; with height 10 ft (matching the shared wall), the hall's length = 300 divided by 10 = 30 ft. The combined outer boundary is then one big rectangle 40 ft (10+30) by 10 ft, so its perimeter = 2 x (40 + 10) = 100 ft.
s: Chooses the bedroom's side (10 ft) and finds its area (100 sq ft)
Finds the required hall area (300 sq ft) and its length (30 ft) given height 10 ft
Identifies the combined shape as a 40 ft by 10 ft rectangle
